old: Anxiety is often a Protector trying to prevent danger, shame, abandonment, failure, exposure, illness, rejection, loss of control, or a feeling it believes would be unbearable. Don’t begin by cross-examining it. Help the body first.
Body first. Inner child second. Inquiry third. Action fourth.
new: Remember that often the anxiety comes from a protector part, a part of yourself who is trying to help you, but who believes you are in danger, or may be shamed, or abandoned, or fail, or be exposed, or become sick, or rejected, or lose control, or suffer something else unbearable. Therefore, instead of an interrogation, start with yourself:
Always work with yourself by first taking care of your body, then your inner child, then some inner inquiry, and then some action:

old: Start with the hand-on-heart, hand-on-solar-plexus practice.
“Little one, you are not alone. You do not have to solve this. I am here now. The adult is listening.”
Don’t recite the words like an incantation you’re hoping the subconscious will grade. Say them the way you’d speak to a frightened child you actually love.
new: Inner child love: Put a hand over your heart, and a hand on your solar plexis, and say lovingly, “Little one, you are not alone. You don’t have to fix this. I’m here now. The adult is listening.” Don’t just say the words, but say them in a way that you are talking to the inner child, who is frightened.

old: Use this gently. Buteyko-style reduced breathing can help some people who overbreathe or panic, but don’t force breath holds. Air hunger can briefly increase anxiety before it settles, so go slowly.
Breathe through the nose. Let the inhale be small. Let the exhale be quiet. Pause only if comfortable. Let the breath become less dramatic. Stop if dizzy, strained, panicky, or medically concerned.
new: Reduce your breathing. (NOTE: there are some good things to be said for slowing down the breathing, for some who overbreathe or are panicked, and this part is based on the Buteyko approach. But please don’t force yourself to hold your breath and suffer air hunger, which is going to make you more anxious for a period. Proceed slowly.) Take small inhales through the nose, and quiet exhales, with pauses if you can. Can you quiet your breathing? STOP if you feel dizzy or experience any other medical issues.

old: EFT can be a simple bodily ritual: name the fear, tap gently, and stay in contact with what you feel. The evidence is still developing. A 2025 systematic review found seven randomized controlled trials involving EFT for anxiety disorders; EFT beat no intervention in several of them, although the evidence should still be treated cautiously beside first-line therapies.
“Even though this anxiety is here, I am willing to be kind to the part of me that is afraid.”
new: EFT tapping: One of the easiest ways to do EFT is to say something like, “Even though I have this anxiety, I am willing to be kind to the part of me that is afraid,” while you tap on your body. There isn’t a ton of evidence for EFT, but there are some studies on anxiety. A 2025 systematic review found 7 randomized control trials for anxiety disorders, and noted that EFT was more effective than no intervention in a few studies. So use the evidence with caution, and know that there are first line therapies for anxiety.

old: More info, and a free intro session on my Somatic Guide. With SE, we track gently. Don’t turn the exercise into trauma excavation.
“Where is the activation?” “Where is the neutral place?” “Can attention move slowly between them?”
new: Somatic experiencing: If you would like more information about somatic experiencing, or even a free intro session, please see my somatic guide . In somatic experiencing (SE), you are not thrusting into the trauma. You learn to track. So you might start by tracking, by discovering where the activation is, where a neutral place is, and then whether you can move your attention from one to the other, very slowly, like a snail.

old: “What is the felt sense of this whole anxiety?”
Don’t answer from the head immediately. Give the body time to form one vague sense of the whole situation, then ask:
“What would this felt sense like me to know?”

Try a word or phrase and check how well it fits the felt sense. Then examine what it suggests about the situation; feeling right doesn’t settle that. Words and bodily attention can help correct each other.
new: Gendlin Focusing: Focusing is another approach where you work with your body. You might say to yourself, “What is the felt sense of this whole anxiety?” Don’t answer with your head; let your body come up with a vague sense of the whole anxiety. Then ask, “What would this felt sense like me to know?” Try a word or a phrase and see if it feels good. But also see if what the word or phrase says is true of the situation. The word may feel ok, but say something that doesn’t fit the situation, or vice versa. Use the words and the body to mutually correct one another.

old: Sometimes the mind is too activated to meditate usefully. Then help through the body: foot, scalp, temple, neck, or shoulder massage; warmth; pressure; a weighted blanket; darkness; familiar calming music; or a massage gun used carefully. Avoid the front of the neck, injuries, numb areas, bruises, inflamed tissue, recent surgery sites, varicose veins, and anything that produces pain, dizziness, tingling, or a symptom that feels wrong.

Other people settle with warmth, darkness, music, massage, weighted blankets, breathwork, familiar objects, or personal relaxation technology. Use the support that actually helps rather than assembling a tiny wellness trade show around the anxiety.

Personal relaxation-tech note: On my ZHoly3O page, I discuss ozonated charcoal “holy water” as one relaxation support, and I also mention Blushield. These remain optional supports. They don’t prove that any inner signal is true. Stabilize the body, listen gently, reality-test, and return to one grounded action.
new: Work with the body. Sometimes the mind is too activated for meditation to help, so you may need to work directly with the body to calm it down. Maybe get a massage, or massage a foot, your scalp, a temple, or the back of the neck, the top of a shoulder, etc. (Avoid massaging the front of the neck. Also avoid massaging injured or numb body parts, or bruised, inflamed, or recently surgically operated on areas, or varicose veins. Also stop if the massage makes the anxiety symptoms worse, or makes you feel bad in any way, such as painful, dizzy, tingly, etc.) There are many other somatic approaches you can try, like heat, pressure, a weighted blanket, darkness, your favorite calming music, a careful use of a massage gun, etc.
You may find that you settle down with some of these things: warmth, darkness, favorite music, massage, a weighted blanket, some breathwork, a favorite object, technology you use to relax, etc.

I have a page on my ZHoly3O product, which is ozonated charcoal, and I use a bit of this “holy water” as one of the things that helps me relax. (See the mention of Blushield on that page, too.) But neither one of those products are necessary. All you really need is to stabilize yourself, and then listen to the messages from your inner realm, reality test those messages, and then take some action.
A script you could use for anxiety is:

old: First, body. Feet, chair, breath, room.
Little one, I am here. Protector, thank you for warning me. You do not have to scream for me to listen.
If there is real action needed, show me one step. If there is no action needed, help the body stand down gently.
I will not abandon the signal. I will not worship the signal. I will listen, test, and act.
new: Where am my body? What are my feet doing? How am I sitting in the chair? How am I breathing? How is my body in the room?
If you can hear me, I want you to know that I am here. Thank you for alerting me. You don’t have to scream. I got your message.

Now if there is something we need to do, show me what the first thing is that we should do, right now. And if there is nothing we need to do, help my body stand down, and know that I am not going to abandon you, but I am also not going to worship you. I am going to listen to you, reality test what you are saying, and then take some action.

old: The subconscious isn’t the enemy. Neither are the body, the sharp analytical mind, or the protector that has been braced for years. Most of them have been trying to help without ever being properly introduced.
new: Start from the basis that the sub, the body, the sharp mind, and the guy who's tensed up and ready for the other shoe to drop for a long time are all not your enemies. Most of them are actually trying to help you.

old: I’m less interested in how deeply you can get hypnotized than whether you become an adult you can trust.
new: Whether or not you can "get hypnotized" very deeply is somewhat irrelevant to whether or not you can become a trustworthy adult.

old: Listen until the kid is willing to come closer. Keep enough small promises that the guards can occasionally sit down. Love yourself enough that thought stops bracing against tenderness, and think clearly enough that love doesn’t drift into fantasy. Then take the practice back into ordinary life, where the adult keeps the promise.
new: Listen to it for as long as it takes until it's comfortable enough to move closer to you. This is easiest to do if you're making and keeping lots of small promises to the kid, so the various guards feel they can relax. Work on loving yourself in a way that your thinking doesn't object to; work on thinking in a way that your love for yourself doesn't become fantasy; work on doing this in the course of regular life so that your adult self can keep the promise.

old: You were born with a mind that can dream, protect, analyze, imitate, love, remember, hide, reveal, and heal. Nobody taught its different layers how to speak to each other.

Instead, most of us learned to push through, suppress emotion, perform confidence, obey or rebel against authority, and call that adulthood. Meanwhile, the deeper mind kept running its own programs: the child wanting safety, the guard expecting danger, the body remembering what the intellect had explained away, the intuition speaking before language, and the fantasy trying to become guidance.

A lot of hypnosis teaching treats the subconscious like a machine waiting for commands. That never did much for me. I get more from sitting down and listening until the scared kid, the guard, the body, the intuition, and the part trying to run Tuesday can all be heard without one of them seizing the microphone.
In this guide, self-hypnosis gathers attention until the conscious mind, subconscious, body, inner child, protectors, adult self, and Higher Self can participate in one honest inner meeting.
The method is simple: listen, warm, protect, clarify, reality-test, and act.
A dramatic trance is optional. The goal is a more trustworthy relationship with the whole mind, proven in ordinary life.

Communion is the closest word I have for that. The conscious mind stops shouting from the roof, and the subconscious no longer has to communicate only through symptoms, dreams, cravings, daydreams, and peculiar little body signals.

I treat the subconscious as a living ecology of parts, memories, impulses, images, protections, and wisdom. I bring in inner-child reparenting because a wounded young part won’t be repaired by a clever suggestion. I begin with Higher Self or the universal heart when the system needs coherence, and separate into parts only when that helps. I borrow from prompt engineering because the shape of a question changes the kind of answer we can hear. And I include influence literacy because hypnosis is hardly the only thing hypnotizing us.
new: Have you ever realized that you were born with an incredible brain/mind that has many layers of consciousness: dream, protect, analyze, imitate, love, remember, hide, show, heal, etc, etc?

Yet you were taught (or you figured out) that the way to ‘grow up’ and be an ‘adult’ is to push through, repress, supress, pretend you’re confident, follow authority, go against authority, etc etc etc, and mind you deeper mind is still running all of the programs it’s running: child mind, guard mind, body mind, intuitive mind, fantasy mind (trying to become guidance mind), etc etc

While some of the teachings on hypnosis talk about the ‘subconscious mind’ like it’s one giant machine you just have to put the right commands into in order to get it to do what you want, for me, the most useful thing to do is talk to the different parts of myself until they can all hear each other.

I teach a self-hypnosis method that allows you to gather all of your attention and have your conscious mind, subconscious mind, body mind, inner child mind, protector part minds, adult mind and Higher Self be able to all hear and talk to each other.

“How do I do this?” you ask. Just listen. When you warm up to what’s there, protect it, clarify what it is, reality test it, and then act on it, you’ll find that you don’t even need to have a ‘trance experience’ to demonstrate the results of all parts of your mind talking to each other and trusting each other more.

I like to think of it like a ‘communion’ between all parts of our mind, where the conscious mind doesn’t have to shout from the roof top and the subconscious mind doesn’t have to manifest symptoms, dreams, cravings, day dreams and weird body signals in order to communicate.

I work with the subconscious as if it were a ecology, and often begin hypnosis working with the Higher Self (universal heart) and only separate into parts when needed. I combine this with inner child reparenting, and also aspects of prompt engineering, as well as helping people to be literate in the domain of what’s hypnotizing them.

old: Suggestibility varies wildly. Some people open more with an external hypnotist, some with themselves, some only in particular states, and some barely respond to commands while responding deeply to imagery, music, metaphor, or spiritual feeling. A professional can bring pacing, containment, and another set of eyes. Self-hypnosis gives you instant follow-up, real-time correction, and a private line to your own protectors.
new: One of the issues here is that people vary dramatically in how suggestible they are, both internally and externally, to various types of suggestion, and different people vary in how suggestible they are in different states. Different types of suggestion (commands, imagery, music, metaphors, spiritual, etc) can be very different for different people. So there are definite advantages to both having someone work with you, and doing things yourself. Being able to follow up immediately, to correct something in real time, to have a line of communication with protectors, etc.

old: Ask what they are trained to treat, how they use hypnosis, and how they respond when a suggestion doesn’t fit. For trauma work, ask about actual trauma and dissociation training, not only a hypnosis certificate. Credentials matter without guaranteeing competent care.

Describe what has helped, what hasn’t, your preferred directness, acceptable touch and imagery, and how you’ll stop. Ask about unexpected reactions, uncertain memories, and the full return. Firm encouragement can fit; refusal still ends it.

Evaluate what actually happened, not the method’s name. Was its purpose explained? Did you agree? How did the practitioner respond to you? Discomfort alone doesn’t settle the question; treating every objection as proof you need more of the same deserves scrutiny. Ask the app or another informed person for explanation, without expecting a practitioner to be certified from a brief account. Self-hypnosis, combined work, or another practitioner remain your choices.
new: What they are trained in (what they can treat) How they use hypnosis What they will do if things don't "fit" (if they are treating trauma, did they have specific training on trauma and dissociation? Having hypnosis certifications doesn't mean they are trained in trauma care)

What has/hasn't worked for you in the past How direct you want them to be What kind of touch (if any) you are ok with What kind of imagery (if any) you are ok with What you want them to do if you want them to stop What they will do if things go unexpected during or after the session What they do if you aren't sure if something is a memory or not How they will do the full return (coming out of hypnosis) at the end of the session You should be able to be firmly encouraged, but not forced to continue if you don't want to.

Then afterwards, check in about what was actually done, regardless of what you might call the method. Ask the person why they did what they did, if they told you in advance. Did you agree to it? How did the person respond to you? Keep in mind that just because something made you uncomfortable, it doesn't mean it was "bad," but if they saw your discomfort as meaning that you needed more of it, that might be something to look into. You might even be able to use this app or ask around to see if someone can tell you what the things they did meant. They probably won't be able to tell you if the person was "certified" in them or not, though. Then you can decide if you want to try learning to do self-hypnosis, using both, or find someone else. Those are all good options.

old: The subconscious can notice things the conscious mind misses: anticipations, pattern reads, and sometimes something uncanny. Respect the signal without turning a vivid image or directive into an order.
When the message has large or irreversible consequences, slow the action to the scale of those consequences, ask the adult questions, and bring the message to a council.
new: Your subconscious is amazing at picking up on things your conscious mind isn't getting. Whether it's anticipations, reading patterns, or just picking up on uncanny things, it's good to respect what your subconscious is picking up on. But just because your subconscious gives you an image or tells you to do something, that doesn't mean you need to treat it like an order.
Especially if it's a big thing, or something that can't be easily undone, slow it down to the scale of the thing. Look at it with your adult's eyes, and take it to council.

old: The first council is internal: child and adult, conscious and subconscious, intuition and analysis. Reach outside when the message is bigger than those parts can hold alone. The larger and less reversible the move, the more seriously you seek other minds.
Ask people who love you, like-minded people, or somebody who has walked the path. Going alone can be legitimate, but I’d make it the last step after counsel was genuinely sought.
new: Ask your child, your adult, your conscious mind, your subconscious mind, your intuition, your analytical mind. But if it's bigger than all of those, ask outside of yourself, too. The bigger and more un-undoable something is, the more you want to reach outside.

Ask people who love you, people who are like you, people who have done what you are thinking of doing. Sometimes it is right to go it alone, but I would suggest making it the last step, after you've tried to get council.

old: Forgiveness can’t be forced. It grows from understanding, and pushing it too early creates bypass. Staying angry forever can also let the injury keep governing the present. All of these can remain true together: the harm happened, the boundary still matters, the person remains accountable, and forgiveness may come later when your relationship to the event changes on its own.
new: You say that we cannot ‘force’ ourselves to forgive someone and that it has to come out of a place of understanding for it to not be a bypass etc. But how can we let go of the anger if we cannot or do not want to always be angry? How do we hold all of this, together? The fact that all of this can be true at the same time is so important.

old: The induction and inner meeting bring you to a place where you can listen. From here, learn to answer what happens instead of reciting a speech that has already decided what every part will say. Read these examples before practicing, then put the screen aside.

Notice one thing accurately. Offer a small, believable invitation, an act of care, or more time. Acknowledge only what actually happens, then wait. A sensation can lead to an image, a gesture, a feeling, or words; you don’t need to fill every category.
new: Once you've read the induction and done the inner meeting, this will make more sense. Read through these, and then try doing it without looking at the screen.

Respond to each thing that comes up with an accurate notice and a small reasonable invitation (or act or taking more time etc). The 'thing' might be a sensation, image, gesture, feeling, words, or anything. The notice and invitation don't need to take all those forms, just notice and invite what happens.

old: Suppose you notice, “My chest tightened when I imagined asking for help.” Start with that, rather than deciding you’ve found an abandoned child or a protective mechanism.
And as I notice that tightening, I can give myself a little time before deciding what it means … and notice whether there’s something I’d like to say, change, or simply stay with.

Then listen. That is enough language for one invitation. A plain “What happens next?” may be better than an elegant sentence. When a feeling is developing, pause the words if that gives it room; keep using them when they help you understand.

You can be firmer when that is the help you chose: “Let the explanation wait a moment. What do I feel as I say that?” Directness can focus attention without deciding the answer. A difficult feeling needn’t become pleasant before you can stay with it. When you remain present, can change direction, and want to continue, sadness or tension alone doesn’t require an exit.

Keep apart what you noticed, what it seemed to mean, and what you think about that meaning now. These can overlap; you don’t need to prove which came first. When useful, ask: “What did I notice? What did it seem to mean? What supports or challenges that interpretation?”

“My stomach tightened” reports a sensation. “That person is evil” is a conclusion—even if it arrived as a wordless certainty. Ask what they actually did, what cues you noticed, and what else could explain the alarm. A sentence you find now can help examine the meaning without being a sentence you thought then. Nonverbal doesn’t mean deeper or truer; earlier doesn’t mean more reliable. Feelings deserve attention, and their meanings remain open to analysis.
new: An example notice might be, "I notice my chest tightening when I imagine asking for help". Don't add interpretation like "this must be the abandoned child part of me, or a protective mechanism" - just notice what you notice. An example invitation might be, "And as I notice that, I can take some time to decide whether that's accurate or not, and notice if I want to say anything, or change it, or just stay like that".

Then just listen. You don't need fancy language - often it will be better to just ask what happens next, or whatever. If you notice a feeling developing, it might be best not to say anything while it's developing (if you can help it) but somedays you need to talk to understand, so just do that.

You can be pretty straightforward when you say you're not going to do something that isn't helping - "That's not helping, I'm not going to do that anymore." can be a perfectly valid thing to say to yourself, and help you focus. It's ok to just be with an unpleasant feeling, you don't have to wait till it's a nice one before you know you're ok. As long as you're ok, and willing to change if you want to, and happy to carry on, a sad feeling or tension or whatever doesn't mean it's not ok.

It's worth trying to separate the notice, the meaning, and your thoughts on the meaning, but in practice it will often be pretty fuzzy. When you can, it can be helpful to separate it out like that though - "I noticed... this seemed to mean... here's why that might be true / false" or something like that.

Is this a notice or meaning? "My stomach went tight" is a notice, "He's a complete bastard" is a meaning, even if you didn't think it in words. You can then go on to find out what he did, notice what it was that gave you the idea, and consider if there might be other explanations. It's also ok to use phrases that you didn't think in your head - if something comes up that you're analysing, it's still good to analyse, even if it's not in your head already. Nonverbal thoughts and early thoughts aren't necessarily any better or worse than other thoughts. Feelings are good to pay attention to, but it's still good to consider what they mean.

old: “My shoulders tightened” and “that wording feels wrong” are different observations. Tightening alone doesn’t explain itself. Ask what happened and whether the invitation fits. An explicit no needs no further justification; change the words, the pace, or the approach. Don’t repeat an unwelcome suggestion more persuasively.
I notice the tightness. I can leave it as it is for a moment. Does this invitation fit, or would I prefer something different?

Sometimes the sentence was simply wrong. Sometimes an unfamiliar possibility brings a feeling worth meeting. You don’t have to decide which before making space to find out. Skepticism is not automatically a protector, and silence is not proof that a hidden process is working.
new: If you notice something like your shoulders tightening in response to an invitation, that's different from saying "that's not quite right". The first one doesn't tell you why - it's worth considering whether it fits, but if you get a clear 'no' then you don't need any more reason to change what you're doing. If something doesn't fit, change it - don't keep trying the same thing.
"I notice the tightness, and I can just leave it like that. I wonder if that fits, or if I'd rather do something different?"
Sometimes it just isn't right - sometimes it's something you hadn't thought of. Neither is a protector, and just being silent doesn't mean there's a process.

old: When another person is involved, notice what they actually do before making the whole problem an inner-child reaction. Can they hear disagreement, take responsibility, and make room for your experience? Keep the judgment specific and revisable; disagreement or a boundary alone doesn’t establish emotional immaturity. You don’t need repeated exposure to danger before protecting yourself.

Notice your side too. Guilt doesn’t prove wrongdoing or manipulation. Did you cause harm that needs repair, abandon your position to make their disappointment go away, or both? Choose a realistic purpose for the next interaction. Sometimes it is mutual understanding; sometimes it is conveying information, saying no, or ending the exchange. You don’t have to make someone understand before you can act.
new: If there is another person involved in the situation, it may be a good idea to look at what they are doing as well. Are they able to communicate in a mature fashion? Try and be specific in your description, and be willing to alter it if you find out that it was incorrect. Just because someone is disagreeing with you or trying to set boundaries around you does not mean they are in their emotionally immature parts. You don’t need to subject yourself to something that may be dangerous to determine if this is the case.

On the other hand, you may find that you have acted inappropriately and you feel guilty. Having feelings of guilt does not mean that you have done something wrong or that you have been manipulated. Have you done something that was wrong or that caused harm? If so, what can you do to fix it? On the other hand, did you give in to someone else just to keep them from being disappointed in you? What do you want to do or achieve the next time you interact with this person? Do you need them to understand what you are feeling/thinking? Do you just need to communicate information to them? Do you need to set boundaries with them? Do you need to end the interaction prematurely?

old: When you need less, widen attention to the room, the chair, a sound, or somewhere in the body that is easier to meet. Let that support become noticeable alongside the difficulty. Moving between difficult and more manageable experience is often called pendulation; approaching in smaller amounts is titration. Use the actual response to set the pace, rather than counting compulsory cycles.
I can let this much be here and notice the support beside it.

Return to the difficult material only when you choose. If you’re losing track of the present, becoming increasingly unreal, or unable to shift or stop, end inward exploration and use the full return. Persistent disorientation needs human help rather than a stronger induction.

An impulse to turn, reach, push away, or change posture can also be explored through a small, voluntary, physically comfortable movement—or imagined without moving. Notice what follows. You’re not obliged to enact an impulse, shake, or produce a release. Stop movement that causes pain or concerning symptoms.
new: When you start to contact it, if it feels too much, immediately start to widen your awareness to something else in the room, in your body, etc. Keep moving back and forth between the difficult thing and the easier thing. This is called pendulation and titration. Do as much or as little as you feel you can. You set the pace, you don’t have to do a certain number.
Ok, I think that is enough for now.

Feel free to go back and explore more if you wish to do so. If, at any point, you start to lose contact with the here and now, feel that things are becoming more and more unreal, or you feel that you are not able to switch to something else or stop, stop trying to explore inside of yourself and just do the entire “coming back” part. If you have trouble orienting yourself and it lasts for a prolonged period of time, please get some human help rather than trying a stronger “induction” back to the here and now.

If you feel an urge to move, turn, reach, push, or change your body’s position, feel free to either actually do something that will not cause your body pain or discomfort, or just imagine doing what you feel you need to do, and see what happens next. You do not need to “act out” the urge, feel that you need to move, shake, release, etc. If you do move and you feel that you are causing yourself pain or other symptoms that you are concerned about, stop moving.

old: When a younger feeling appears, offer company without making it become literally younger or explain its history. When a protector is recognizable, listen to its concern without demanding that it step aside. No part is exiled from the meeting, and none has to disappear or trust you immediately.
I’m here. Would company help, or would you prefer some space?

“Don’t come closer” is information you can act on. Stay at the chosen distance and notice what receiving that response is like. The Nurturer can change the tone; the Protector can carry out a boundary; the Leader can point toward the life you want. They don’t each need a speech. When a capacity isn’t available, borrow that one function. Use the Witness only if you need it to begin; don’t restart a step you can already do.

You can also deliberately try support: a welcome hand placement, an imagined presence, words you’d like to hear, a different posture, or more distance. Introduce one change and discover its effect. A comforting-sounding resource earns its place by helping this person now.

Care can bring grief for what was missing. That needn’t mean the love failed. Stay with the response when you want to and can remain present; more tears don’t prove more healing. If this particular voice, closeness, touch, or image feels intrusive, change it before concluding that you can’t receive love.

A metaphor can develop before you decide what it means. “If this problem had its own image or story, what would appear—and what wants to happen next?” Try only the missing resource, boundary, distance, or action that seems useful. The result is symbolic information or a hypothesis, never proof of history.

Or spend the session developing love, play, courage, or curiosity. Let a pleasant experience have time to grow. Rehearse a chosen action and notice what it would take to carry it out. Hypnosis can invite something new as well as listen to what is already present.
new: If any “younger” parts come up, offer them the opportunity to spend time with you. You don’t have to consider them literally “younger”, nor do you have to ask them why they are there or what happened to them. If you can identify any “protector” parts, talk to them and find out what they are concerned about. All of them are welcome to the “meeting”. You don’t have to get rid of any of them.

If you feel that it would be useful to bring in a “nurturer”, “protector”, “leader”, etc to help you either change the “tone” of the interaction, set boundaries, or help you figure out how to live your life in a better fashion, feel free to do so. You don’t have to talk to them, just use them to get whatever function you need that you aren’t able to do on your own. You only need to use the “Witness” if you need help getting started with a step. If you are already able to do a certain step, you don’t have to do it again.

Try some different ideas as to what might be helpful for this ‘inner part’ to feel better (being welcomed by you, visualising someone else, giving them the sort of words they would like to hear, you placing yourself in a different body position, you moving further away etc). Only try one idea at a time to see if it works. Just because an idea ‘should’ be a resource, that doesn’t mean that it will be.

It is possible that when you try and give the part what it wants, you might feel very upset. It may be that it never got what it needed at the time and now that you are giving it what it wants, it is processing the upset of not getting what it wanted before. If this happens, allow yourself to respond for as long as you want to do so, and for as long as you can ‘stay there’ (ie remain in the process). If you feel that the voice, distance, touch, image etc is too much, then change it to something that is less. Don’t think that you can’t ‘take’ the love.

Allow yourself to see where the metaphor takes you. Ask questions like ‘if the problem had an image or story, what would it be?’ or ‘what would need to happen to make things right?’ If it feels like you need to ‘do something’ to give yourself the resource that you feel you need (or to put a boundary in place, or to move away or to take some other action) then try ‘doing that’ for as far as it takes to be of use to you. Remember that whatever you find out, is likely to be metaphorical. It may be a good hypothesis for what you need to do but it is not a proven fact.

Alternatively, you may want to use the session to develop a capacity that you want to develop (ie love, play, courage, curiosity etc). You can also use it to rehearse something that you have decided to do.

old: When you’ve received enough, stop opening new questions. Ask what would help you leave this here for now. Thank the parts or capacities you worked with, in whatever words you can mean. A meal, a boundary, rest, a repaired relationship, or a promise kept may matter more than another insight. There needn’t be an action when none is called for.

Keep the analytical mind available throughout: you can question, disagree, and stop. Save extended factual checking and consequential commitments for after the return. An image can be meaningful without being a historical memory; a bodily shift or relief doesn’t make an interpretation true.

Use Come all the way back, even when you ended early. Afterwards, write a few lines: what was there before; what I tried; what happened; what remains uncertain. Include a phrase, bodily signal, child’s need, protector’s concern, boundary, repair, or what not to force only when it actually appeared. You don’t owe the notebook a complete cast of characters.
new: Ending the session . Don’t feel that you have to end the session with a ‘great revelation’! When you have done as much as you want to do, it is a good idea to find out if there is anything that you need to do to make sure that you can leave things where they are for the time being. This might include thanking parts for their help, or making sure that you do something ‘in real life’ (eat a good meal, put a boundary in place, get some rest, repair a relationship, keep a promise etc) or it may be that there is nothing to do!

Note : throughout the exercise, allow your ‘analytical’ part to make comments and/or tell you that it doesn’t like what you are doing and/or tell you to stop doing the exercise. Just tell it that you will check things out when you come back and make any commitments etc when you are back. Remember that the images that you see are unlikely to be actual memories of things that happened and just because you see an image, or feel a body release, that doesn’t mean that you are right about what is going on!

Just jot down the essentials (what was there before you started, what you have done to change things, what you are unsure about, any phrases that were said, any body signals, any information that the ‘inner child’ said that it needed, anything that a ‘protector’ wanted you to know, any boundaries that you put in place, any ‘repairs’ that you did, anything that you learnt about what it is a mistake to try and force etc). Wonder, play, vivid sensation, vulnerability, honest need, or the wish to carry fewer decisions can all come forward while the internal adult remains present.
new: It’s possible to let the ‘younger’ parts of you express themselves without surrendering your adult judgement to them, and without literally reverting to a younger age. Instead, the aim is to access the positive aspects of ‘younger’ feeling states, such as a sense of wonder or playfulness, more direct sensory experiences, vulnerability, need, and a desire to let someone else make decisions for you.

old: When love is available, the younger state doesn’t have to believe in it before you can offer it. Trust can question your promises, remember failures of protection, and take its time. Love can remain present while that happens.
“Okay. I believe that you don’t believe me. I still love you. You don’t have to love me back. Tell me what feels unsafe.”

That isn’t a way to end the complaint. Listen for what is true in it and answer seriously. Hearing anger without retaliation, admitting a real failure, and repairing after an internal attack are evidence alongside meals, boundaries, appointments, and kept promises. Non-retaliation expresses love; it shouldn’t replace love with a colder performance of good behavior.

Notice what each position teaches the others. A vow followed by blame when it is doubted teaches that love depends on receiving it correctly. The blaming voice and the voice making the vow may be different positions, the same position, or a blend. Don’t decide from the person’s chronological age.

When a younger version of you becomes the defendant, ask what they understood then, what options they could see and tolerate, and what happened because of the choice. Harm can require responsibility and repair. Punishment cannot retroactively create the capacity that was missing.
new: Even if your inner child does not believe that you love him or her, you can still love him or her.
You can say, out loud or in your head, “Okay. I believe that you don’t believe me, but I still love you. You don’t have to love me back. Please tell me what is not okay with you.”

Respond to complaints, which are likely to include something true. Showing that you love him or her can include some or all of the following: listening to him or her when he or she is angry without hitting back, owning up to what was not okay, working on being less likely to turn on him or her, and other ways of making it up to him or her. Other ways of showing that you love him or her include taking care of him or her by buying and cooking food, setting limits, taking him or her to doctor’s appointments, and doing what you say you will do. Just not hitting back is not enough; you also need to love your inner child.

Be aware of what you are teaching your other positions. You might be teaching your inner child that you are going to love him or her no matter what, but you might also be teaching him or her that he or she is responsible for believing your love, and that if he or she does not, it is his or her fault. The position that is making the vow to love the inner child no matter what, and the position that is blaming the inner child for not taking in the love, might be separate positions, or they might be one position, or you might be blending them. It might not be based on chronological age.

When you're placing your younger self on trial, how valuable is it for you to consider how valuable it might have been for your younger self at the time to be doing what they did, given what they knew at the time? How valuable is it for you to consider how valuable it might have been for them to think what they thought, given what they thought at the time? How valuable is it for you to consider what options were available to them at the time, and how tolerable they were? How valuable is it for you to consider the consequences of their actions at the time? How valuable is it for you to consider that whilst their actions might have caused harm to you and others, punishing yourself now will not give them the capacity they needed at the time, and that it is more useful to work on what you can do now to deal with the harm that was caused?
WORKING WITH YOUR INNER CHILD:

old: Place one hand at the center of the chest as a physical connection to love. Put the other at the solar plexus, just beneath the chest, where you can relate to the vulnerable child.

Send warmth from the heart toward the child. Notice whatever comes back—a sensation, image, feeling, resistance, or nothing—and answer with warmth again. Let it become a conversation rather than a performance.
Love above. Child below. Adult present.
new: There is a simple and easy body technique to connect with your inner child. Just place one hand in the center of your chest which is physically connecting you to your love and then place your other hand just below that which is your solar plexis and where your child can be.

Begin to send love from your heart down to your child and just notice what comes up for you. It doesn't matter if something comes up or not. If you feel resistance, just meet it with love. If you feel or see something, just meet that with love as well. This is a conversation with your child from your heart.
Remember, Love is on top, your child is on the bottom and you are there with them.

old: The Nurturer brings warmth without trying to rush the feeling away, and takes pleasure in the child’s company: “I’m glad you’re here.” The child needs to be enjoyed, not only comforted when hurt.
“It’s okay to feel this.” “I’m here.” “You don’t have to do anything right now.” “You are not too much.” “You can be small here.” “You can be angry here.” “You can be sad here.” “I will stay.”
new: THE NURTURER: As a Nurturer one of the most important things that you can do is to enjoy your inner child, to sit back and not feel like you have to move their feelings and to say to them that you are really glad that they are here in this moment. Children need to be enjoyed.
It’s okay that you’re feeling the way you are feeling.
I want you to know I’m here for you.
You don’t need to do anything right now.
It’s okay that you’re not too much. It’s okay to be small. You can be small here.
It’s okay to be angry. You can be angry here.
It’s okay to be sad. You can be sad here.

old: The Protector turns warmth into something the child can believe.

“I will set the boundary.” “I will leave the unsafe conversation.” “I will stop texting the person who destabilizes us.” “I will eat.” “I will sleep.” “I will keep a small promise.” “I will not leave the child alone with adult consequences.”

This is where inner-child practice often turns decorative. The voice says loving things while the adult sends the destabilizing message, skips the meal, avoids the task, and breaks the promise. Trust begins when you handle the consequence.

If warmth is unavailable, a protective act can begin the relationship. Make it small enough to carry out and review what actually happened. A missed action might reflect fear, exhaustion, missing skills, a practical barrier, or a poor plan. Completion without immediate relief isn’t automatically failure, and a tick on a list doesn’t prove the action helped.
new: I’m going to be here for you.
The Protector:

Work with your Protector to set boundaries together. They might be small, like “I’m going to leave this conversation because it’s not safe,” or “I’m going to stop texting someone who destabilizes me.” They might be self-care related, like “I’m going to eat” or “I’m going to get sleep.” They might be trust-related, like “I’m going to keep this promise to myself” or “I’m not going to leave you alone to deal with these adult things.”

A lot of inner child work fails because we do all the fluffy stuff, but then we go text the person who destabilizes us or don’t eat or don’t do whatever thing we were meant to be doing. Trust comes from being able to handle adult things.

If you can’t bring up the warmth stuff yet, that’s okay, you can always do something to be protective of your inner child. Make sure they’re small enough that you can do them. If you can’t, figure out what’s getting in the way of doing them. Are you scared? Tired? Don’t know how? Is there a practical obstacle in your way? Did you set yourself up to do it successfully? Be careful not to define doing the thing successfully as “feeling good about it” or “being able to check it off a list.”

old: The Leader gives direction. You can call this function Leader, Guide, Guru, Wise One, Sage, Inner Teacher, Director, or Higher Adult. The label matters much less than the ability to orient the whole system toward a life.

Direction can ask for something difficult without turning life into perfect discipline and hidden needs. Sometimes the next adult move is asking for help, expressing a preference, or letting a safe person see an imperfection. Wanting closeness is legitimate; punishing someone for needing space is a different strategy. Find a way to meet the need without erasing either person.

“We are not only here to feel better.” “We are here to become whole.” “We are here to belong to life itself, not only to people who approve of us.” “We are here to serve truth, beauty, love, God, source, nature, universe, dharma, Tao, and the benefit of all beings.”
Begin with the adult function you can actually reach. Protection may come before warmth. Direction should help the child grow without erasing care, play, or support.
new: The Leader/Guide/Guru:
You can also work with your Leader. Call them whatever you want, Guide, Guru, Wise One, Sage, Inner Teacher, Director, Higher Adult, whatever.

Ask them for help with directing your life. Be careful not to ask for the kind of “tough it out, you don’t have needs, you just need discipline!” kind of direction, though. Ask them for help in directing you to do adult things in a way that takes your needs into account: asking for the help you need, expressing your preferences, letting someone see you in an imperfect way, finding ways to get your need for closeness met without punishing someone for their need for space, etc. etc.

Affirmations might be helpful here, too: “We’re not just here to feel good. We’re here to become whole. We’re here to be part of life. We’re here to serve truth/beauty/love/God/source/nature/the universe/dharma/the Tao/the benefit of all beings,” etc. etc.

Start with whatever adult function you can connect to. Even if you start with protection and can’t do the warmth stuff yet, make sure the direction you’re being led in is appropriate for your inner child’s growth (i.e. not depriving them of things they need, like play or support, etc.)

old: Use this parts language when you actually recognize a protective pattern or find it useful to explore. A sensation, distraction, or objection doesn’t establish its cause. Notice it first; hunger may need food, skepticism may be reasonable, and a sentence may simply not fit.
new: Working with protectors:

Feel free to use parts language here, too, if it’s helpful. Often, we see a sensation or a distraction or an objection as something that needs to be explored, when in fact it might just be hunger, or reasonable skepticism about something, or a sentence that doesn’t fit. It’s good to notice it, though, and then to see what might be going on.

old: “I notice you. You are trying to protect something. I want to understand. What are you afraid would happen if you stopped?”

Then wait. The answer may be: “You’ll lie to yourself again.” “This will become another performance.” “If you feel the pain, you’ll be destroyed.” “You’ll use spirituality to avoid reality.” “You’ll forgive too early.” “You’ll call fantasy guidance.” “You’ll abandon us as soon as the session ends.”
“That makes sense. You do not have to move yet. What would help you trust me 1% more?”

Usually the protector needs evidence more than another spiritual insight. Hold the boundary. Handle the task. Eat the meal. Don’t send the message. Keep the promise. Sleep. Contact the therapist. Acknowledge the debt. Write down the truth.
new: (“I notice you and what you are trying to do. I want to know more. Could I ask you what you are afraid would happen if you stopped protecting me by…..?)

If necessary take time and listen. (Perhaps they are afraid that you will lie to yourself again or pretend again or that it will be too painful or you will get spiritual bypass again or you will forgive someone who shouldn’t be forgiven yet or you will see what you want to see or that you will leave them hanging after the session or…..)

(Now talk to the protector. Tell them that it makes sense that they want to protect you and that they don’t have to stop protecting you, but that you want to know what could make them trust you 1% more that you can do that.)

Most of the time the protector wants you to do certain things, set boundaries, do whatever you are supposed to do, eat, not text someone, keep a promise, go to sleep, talk to the therapist, admit that you owe someone money, write something down, etc.

old: The Protector is more than an inner voice saying no. You can practice it as a bodily sequence:
Orient: look around and feel the support beneath you.
Assess: ask what is known, what is uncertain, and what needs checking.
Distinguish: separate present danger from uncertainty, old alarm, or imagined danger.
Set one proportionate boundary: move, stop, delay, ask, leave, or get support.
Verify enough safety: not perfect certainty, just enough reality-based evidence for the next step.
Stand down and rest: protection includes ending the scan when continued vigilance is no longer helping.

A mature Protector can say, “I don’t know.” It can ask another human, delay interpretation, or choose a no-trance practice. I’m aiming for discernment that acts when needed and then quits scanning the room after the danger has passed.
new: Do you want to “embody” your Protector? Then you could practice this:
1. orient self (look around, feel the support around you, etc.)
2. assess the situation (know what you know, what you don’t know and check out what you need to)
3. differentiate between actual/real danger, unknown, past or imagined dangers
4. set boundaries (start with one and make it relative to the danger; move, stop, delay, ask, leave, get support, etc.)
5. verify if it is safe enough
6. stand down and rest

This seems to me like a “mature” Protector. One that is not afraid to say that he doesn’t know, or one that can ask another human being, or one that can delay interpreting a situation or one that can use a no-trance method. I want to be able to “do” this too. I am learning to “do” discernment when I need to and stop scanning the room when it isn’t needed anymore.

old: I connect my reparenting therapy to self-hypnosis because I find they are a perfect match. The child may arrive as an age, image, posture, voice, memory, emotion, or plain vulnerability. Sometimes no child appears. Stay with a recognizable protector, or with the sensation, feeling, or preference that is actually present.
When the child does appear, resist the urge to begin a healing project immediately. Be with them first.
“Little one, I am here. You do not have to explain everything. You do not have to be healed today. You do not have to become impressive. I only want to know what would help you feel less alone.”
The need may be warmth, play, protection, grief, anger, food, rest, a boundary, a safer relationship, less fantasy, less overwork, or one adult promise kept today.
new: I see a lot of connection between reparenting therapy and self hypnosis. They fit well together. When you go into hypnosis the child might come to you. If you want, you can see that child in any form you want. It can be an image, a posture, a voice, a memory, an emotion, etc. It can be any age you want it to be. It can be any vulnerable part of you. It doesn’t even have to be a “child”, if there is no child there, just work with a protector or whatever you find.

old: When a younger state, protector, feeling, or bodily signal needs care, move patiently:
Prepare: create enough time, privacy, support, and adult capacity.
Inspect: notice what is present before deciding what it means.
Ask permission: “May I come closer, or would you prefer warmth, space, words, silence, or no contact?”
Respond to one need: do the smallest useful thing rather than attempting a total repair.
Wait: let the response settle. Some changes need quiet, sleep, or ordinary time.
Reconnect: invite contact only where it is welcome. No part has to merge, disappear, forgive, or become cheerful.
Rest: stop before care becomes another performance.
Reassess: return later and ask what actually helped.

The goal isn’t “good as new,” as though history should disappear. Aim for good as you: more supported and connected while still recognizably yourself. If parts language makes you feel more divided, use signals, feelings, younger states, or another metaphor that helps.
new: Just be with the child.
If you can, tell the child that you are there for them and that they don’t have to explain themselves, or be “healed” or impress you. Just tell you what they need to not be alone anymore.

It can be anything. What does the child need? warmth, to play, to be protected, to mourn, to be angry, food, rest, boundaries, better relationships, to stop fantasizing, to stop working their butt off, that you keep a promise to them for one day, etc. etc.
Don't rush it.
Find a younger you/protector/feeling/signal that comes up in your body, and
A. Prepare yourself to tend to them (get yourself into a place where you can spend time with them, have privacy, feel you can access support if you need it, and be as adult as you can be).
B. Look at what's there before judging or deciding what it is.

C. Ask them what you can do or if you can move closer to them. If you feel like you already know what they need, tell them that you're going to get them what they need- warmth, space, verbal reassurance, silence, distance, whatever.
D. Give them what you can- don't feel like you have to fix it all.
E. Give yourself some time to let what you did sink in- it may take some time, it may take you to go to sleep, etc.
F. Reconnect with them- don't expect them to merge, go away, forgive you, become happy, etc. Just reconnect with them if they're willing.
G. Rest, and reconnect with them later to see what was helpful.

Remember the goal isn't to make yourself good as new but to make yourself good as you- more supported and connected to yourself. Feel free to modify this as needed, and if you don't like the idea of part work you can substitute whatever part you're working with for a signal or a feeling, or an imaginary younger you that you feel embodies the issue you're having.

old: Reparenting doesn’t have to become solemn. A younger state may respond to texture, drawing, movement, a plushie with a voice, or whatever feels interesting. Keep reality-testing intact. You’re recovering play, not becoming somebody’s child, pet, doll, or owned object.

Rest also doesn’t require helplessness. Reduce decisions for a defined period, put unfinished tasks somewhere visible, and let the internal adult keep watch. You remain able to move, stop, and return.
new: When you're reparenting, it's okay to play with things that interest your younger states. Whether that means touching things of different textures, drawing, exercising, roleplaying with a plushie in a different voice, etc. As long as you're reality testing is good and you remember that you aren't a child or pet or doll or whatever and that nobody owns you, it's okay to work on getting your play ability back.

When you're resting, you don't have to be helpless. It's okay to cut down the amount of decisions you make for a set period of time, put things you haven't finished on a list where you can see it, and let the adult part of you watch over you.

old: When speech or visualization feels fake, write. Let the non-dominant hand speak for the child or protector, awkward handwriting and all. Answer with the dominant hand as the adult.
Non-dominant hand: “I don’t trust you.”
Dominant hand: “I hear that you don’t trust me. I still love you. Tell me where I’ve let you down. I won’t demand trust; I’ll listen and keep one small promise today.”
Non-dominant hand: “Which promise?”
Dominant hand: “I will eat, clean the desk, and not text the person who makes us feel unsafe.”
new: If talking out loud or visualizing conversations feels fake, try writing it out. Tell your child/ protector part to write with your nondominant hand, and talk to them with your dominant. It might be a little hard to write with your nondominant hand but you can kind of do it. So for example, they might say "I don't trust you" with your nondominant hand, and you can say with your dominant hand "I know you don't trust me right now but I love you and I want to know how I've fucked up. I don't expect you to trust me but I want to hear you out and give you a promise I can keep today" and they can say "what promise?" and you can say "I'm going to make sure I eat today/ clear off my desk/ not text so-and-so"
